name: Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (group 2)

reference.source: ESC/ERS Guidelines for Pulmonary Hypertension / Braunwald's Heart Disease
clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of pulmonary hypertension overall, arising from left heart disease including heart failure with reduced or preserved ejection fraction and valvular disease
Defined haemodynamically as post-capillary, with a raised mean pulmonary artery pressure and an elevated pulmonary artery wedge pressure at right heart catheterisation
Distinguished from pre-capillary disease chiefly by the elevated wedge pressure, which reflects raised left-sided filling pressures transmitted backward
May be isolated post-capillary or combined post- and pre-capillary, the latter carrying a worse prognosis when a superimposed pulmonary vascular component develops
Clues favouring a left heart cause include older age, hypertension, atrial fibrillation, obesity, diabetes, left atrial enlargement, and preserved-ejection-fraction physiology
Treatment is directed at the underlying left heart disease with decongestion and risk-factor control, not at group 1 targeted vasodilators
Targeted pulmonary arterial hypertension therapy is generally not indicated and may cause harm through pulmonary oedema
reference.pathophysiology: Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease is a post-capillary disorder driven by elevated left-sided filling pressures. Systolic or diastolic left ventricular dysfunction, or left-sided valvular disease, raises left atrial and pulmonary venous pressure, which is transmitted backward into the pulmonary capillaries and arteries, producing a passive rise in pulmonary artery pressure while the wedge pressure remains elevated. Over time, chronic pulmonary venous congestion can trigger vasoconstriction and structural remodelling of the pulmonary arteries, adding a pre-capillary component and producing combined post- and pre-capillary disease in which pulmonary vascular resistance also rises. This superimposed arteriopathy further loads the right ventricle and worsens outcome. Because the primary problem is upstream in the left heart, therapy that dilates the pulmonary arteries can increase transpulmonary flow into a congested left heart and precipitate pulmonary oedema.
additionalDifferentials: Idiopathic or heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease or hypoxia (group 3)
Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease mimicking post-capillary congestion
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography to assess left ventricular function, valves, and left atrial size
Right heart catheterisation to document the elevated wedge pressure defining post-capillary disease
Fluid or exercise provocation at catheterisation to unmask occult preserved-ejection-fraction heart failure
Natriuretic peptides and assessment of volume status
Cardiac MRI or ischaemia evaluation where the left heart cause is unclear
Ventilation-perfusion scan and lung imaging to exclude thromboembolic and parenchymal contributors
redFlags: Acute decompensation with pulmonary oedema and hypoxaemia
A disproportionately high pulmonary vascular resistance suggesting a superimposed pre-capillary component
Signs of low cardiac output or cardiogenic shock
Clinical deterioration after inappropriate use of group 1 targeted vasodilators
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is largely determined by the underlying left heart disease, and the development of pulmonary hypertension, particularly a combined post- and pre-capillary pattern, marks more advanced disease and a worse outlook. Optimising treatment of the left heart condition can lower pulmonary pressures, whereas an established pulmonary vascular component is less reversible.
pitfalls: Misclassifying post-capillary disease as pulmonary arterial hypertension and prescribing group 1 targeted therapy
Relying on echocardiographic pressure estimates without catheterisation to determine the wedge pressure
Missing occult preserved-ejection-fraction heart failure by not performing provocation testing
Attributing all the pulmonary hypertension to the left heart when a significant pre-capillary component coexists
Overlooking treatable valvular disease as the driver of pulmonary venous hypertension
references: ESC/ERS Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hypertension
management: Treat the underlying left heart disease as the mainstay: guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and management of hypertension, valvular lesions and preserved-ejection-fraction physiology
Relieve pulmonary venous congestion with diuretic-based decongestion and dietary sodium and fluid moderation
Control contributing risk factors, including blood-pressure optimisation, rate or rhythm control and anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, and management of obesity and diabetes
Avoid group 1 targeted pulmonary vasodilators, which can precipitate pulmonary oedema in post-capillary disease
Monitor with serial echocardiography, natriuretic peptides and functional assessment to track right ventricular load and congestion
Refer for valve repair or replacement where significant left-sided valvular disease drives the pulmonary hypertension
Escalate advanced or combined post- and pre-capillary disease to a specialist pulmonary hypertension and heart failure centre, considering advanced heart failure therapies or transplantation
